tagline: Follow the Okanogan River past towns once served by an earlier highway.
intro: The Okanogan Trails Scenic Byway follows Highway 97 for 80 miles between the Canadian border and Pateros. State of Washington Tourism presents it as a drive through open landscapes and small towns, with history and outdoor recreation along the way. The tourism office gives the drive two hours; part of the route traces the western edge of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation.

The road from Pateros to Okanogan entered the state system in 1905, and the extension to the Canadian border followed in 1907. It formed part of the Wenatchee-Oroville Road, numbered State Road 10. The US 97 number arrived in 1926, when the United States established its numbered highway system. US 97 originally passed through central Okanogan, Omak and Riverside on the west side of the river. A new alignment shifted traffic east of the river and bypassed Okanogan and Omak.

Traveling south, begin beside Osoyoos Lake and pass through Oroville, then follow the river toward Tonasket. Between Tonasket and Riverside, the highway crosses the river and uses Wagonroad Coulee. Beyond the Omak and Okanogan bypasses, it rounds Soap Lake Mountain and reaches the Fort Okanogan area before Brewster. The drive ends at Pateros, where the Methow meets the Columbia.
notice: Oroville’s downtown includes historic buildings and public art.

moments.title: Oroville
moments.text: In 1892 it became Oro, the Spanish word for gold, in an effort to attract prospectors and merchants. The Post Office objected because Washington already had an Oso, and Oro became Oroville in 1909. Rail connections changed too: a branch south to Wenatchee opened in 1914 to avoid the steep inclines of the original Spokane track. US 97 now runs through town at the south end of Osoyoos Lake, where the lake empties into the Okanogan River. Great Northern passenger trains served Oroville until July 14, 1953; freight service continued afterward.

moments.title: Omak
moments.text: Downtown Omak has murals and preserved landmarks, while US 97 bypasses the city center. The city operates a Main Street Historical Tour in its central business district. Its Omak Stampede began in 1933 and takes place on the second weekend of August. The event includes the Suicide Race, in which horses and riders descend a 62-degree slope to the Okanogan River. Horses undergo veterinary examinations and a swim test; animal-welfare organizations have opposed the race over concerns for the horses. SR 215 provides local access through Omak and neighboring Okanogan, linking the bypass to the towns.

moments.title: Fort Okanogan
moments.text: The original Fort Okanogan site lies beneath Lake Pateros, flooded in 1967 after construction of Wells Dam. John Jacob Astor’s Pacific Fur Company established the post in 1811 at the meeting of the Okanogan and Columbia rivers. The North West Company acquired it in 1813, and Hudson’s Bay Company took over after the companies merged in 1821. The buildings had disappeared by 1880, well before the reservoir. The separate interpretive center became part of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation’s History/Archaeology Program after the park transferred out of state ownership in 2011.
